title.narrative: Speak Up! Local Voices for Global Impact

description.narrative:
Speak Up! will educate and empower young people living in rural areas to be active in civic life and learn how to make policy change to improve their local communities through the learning and practice of 4 engagement techniques: grassroots and community, digitaltools, creative techniques, institutional/governmental engagement. Each technique reflects the expertise of 1 partner who will leadits training.
First, partners receive project management training, then youth workers join an online workshop about rural youth national realities, then an in-person training in Senegal for rural young people on the 4 techniques, ending with a 1-month national advocacy campaign using 1 technique from the workshop about 1 issue from the online workshop.
Rural youth are people under 30 with limited opportunities due to their location, including rural or peri-urban areas.
Speak Up! will empower marginalised rural young people across the EU and AU to become skilled, motivated, and connected to influence policy that affect their local realities. It seeks to strengthen grassroots youth advocacy capacity, foster sustainable EU–AU youth networks, and improve policies by amplifying rural youth voices at local, national, regional, and international levels.
In the short term, participants will gain and practice different advocacy methods, practical skills in designing and evaluating advocacy actions, and greater confidence to engage with stakeholders and policymakers.
In the medium term, rural young people will actively participate in policy dialogues and consultations, leador contribute to advocacy campaigns, and strengthen the advocacy capacity of their organisations and communities. Youth organisations will also have greater capacity to engage with policymakers and institutions to increase the awareness of rural youth perspectives, and improve the communication channels between policymakers and rural youth.
In the long term, the project will contribute to the meaningful inclusion of rural youth in governance, more youth-responsive and context-sensitive policies, reduced marginalisation, and stronger democratic participation. The project will deepen EU-AU peer-learning networks, enhance cross-cultural understanding, and initiate youth-led advocacy actions addressing local rural challenges.

participating-org.narrative:
International Falcon Movement - Socialist Education International (IFM-SEI) is an umbrella organisation of 46youth organisations from across 4 continents, working together as a global youth movement to educate andempower young people to take an active role in society and peacefully fight for their rights. The mission of IFM-SEI is to contribute to the education of young people, through socialist values and non-formal education,enabling children and young people to become critical thinkers and active decision-makers in their lives andcommunities.IFM-SEI interprets 'socialist values' as equality, democracy, peace, solidarity, co-operation, anti-capitalism andfriendship, with our 3 central principles of non-formal education, feminism, and equality and inclusion guiding allour decision making.
The following bodies make up the structure and organisation of the IFM-SEI, ranked in decision making order: Congress, International Committee, Presidium, Control Commission.
The Secretariat is the operational epicenter of IFM-SEI, based in Brussels and oversees the daily operations and coordination of the office, implementing the strategic work plan, and managing working groups. The Presidium oversees the advocacy work and successful completion of the Strategy and Work Plan. The Control Commission ensures the compliance with the constitution and financial monitoring. The Secretary General acts as the communication and logistical link between all bodies, unifying the planning and implementation of actions. The two top decision makers, the President and Secretary General, are both under 30 years and the entire Secretariat is under 35 years.
IFM-SEI receives funding through membership fees, donations, and institutional grants, mainly from European Union and Council of Europe.
